Compute blocking indices per participant

Source: R/fba-blocking.R
index_blocking.Rd

Turns the per-trial blocking scores from score_blocking() into two blocking indices per participant over the test blocks selected: the confidence-weighted choice score of Beesley and Le Pelley (2011) and the choice-proportion score of Paskewitz and Jones (2020). See details for their definitions.

Usage

index_blocking(scores, blocks = 1L, by_block = FALSE, silence = FALSE)

Arguments

scores

Per-trial blocking scores; the result from score_blocking().

blocks

Integer. Test blocks that enter the indices. Defaults to 1L, the first test block. NULL selects every block present in scores.

by_block

Logical(1). FALSE (default) pools the selected blocks into one row per participant; TRUE gives one row per participant and selected block, which allows following the indices across the test stage.

silence

Logical(1). Suppress the message about the definitions and the data that entered. Defaults to FALSE (recommended).

Value

A tibble with one row per participant (and selected block, with by_block = TRUE) and columns:

id

Participant identifier.

blocks

The selected blocks as a label, e.g. "1" or "1-6"; with by_block = TRUE, the block of the row.

first_block, last_block, n_blocks

The selected blocks the participant has trials in.

n_trials

Number of test trials in selected blocks.

n_timed_out

Number of trials that ended without a response.

n_answered

Number of trials with a response.

complete

Logical TRUE iff every selected block is present and every trial in it answered.

p_blocking_consistent

Proportion of answered trials consistent with blocking.

bi_confidence

Confidence-weighted choice score: mean signed confidence over answered trials. NA in a design without confidence ratings.

bi_choice

Choice-proportion score: sum over test pairs of the proportion of answers consistent with blocking, minus one half per pair. NA when a pair has no answered trial in the selected blocks.

Participants without any trial in the selected blocks keep a row, with zero counts and NA indices.

Details

Confidence-weighted choice score (bi_confidence)

$$\mathbb{E}[Conf \times (I_{\{o_c\}} - I_{\{o_b\}})]$$

where \(o_c\) is the Stage 3 outcome paired with the control cue, \(o_b\) outcome paired with the blocked cue, and Conf is the confidence rating. The index is thus essentially the mean of signed_confidence. Positive values indicate blocking. The confidence scale bounds the index (-10 to 10 on the 1-to-10 scale of Beesley & Le Pelley, 2011). On the first test block (blocks = 1L), it is the index that Beesley and Le Pelley (2011) reported.

Choice-proportion score (bi_choice)

Paskewitz and Jones (2020, Eq. 24) defined

$$\sum_{p \in P_3} P(o_3 | p) - \sum_{p \in P_4} P(o_3 | p)$$

where \(P_3\) are the test pairs on which blocking predicts \(o_3\) and \(P_4\) those on which it predicts \(o_4\). In other words, \(P_3\) contains those cue compounds, in which the putatively blocked cue was associated with o4 during Stage 3 (i.e., blocking-consistent response on those trials is o3) and vice versa for \(P_4\).

Since \(P(o_3|p)\) is the proportion of consistent answers on the pairs of \(P_3\) and one minus it on the pairs of \(P_4\), and the two sets are equally large, the index equals the sum over all pairs of the proportion of consistent answers minus one half, which is what is computed here. It ranges from -4 to 4 with eight pairs; positive values indicating blocking. Every pair weighs the same, however many of its trials were answered.

Dropped trials

Timed-out trials have no response and do not enter either index; they are counted in n_timed_out. Both indices therefore average over the answered trials only, and a participant with timed-out trials can have more answers expecting one outcome than the other. complete marks the participants without such an imbalance.

Messages

Every call states the blocks that entered, the definitions and sign of the indices, and the participants with timed-out trials or missing blocks, unless silenced (silence = TRUE).

References

Beesley, T., & Le Pelley, M. E. (2011). The influence of blocking on overt attention and associability in human learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes, 37(1), 114-120. doi:10.1037/a0019526

Paskewitz, S., & Jones, M. (2020). Dissecting EXIT. Journal of Mathematical Psychology, 97, 102371. doi:10.1016/j.jmp.2020.102371
